# Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

Junkai Zhou    Jiajia Wu    Zhaoyi Zhang    Shiting Guan    Chuanguang
Yang

###### Abstract

As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers,
automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and
quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model
feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model
expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer
reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable
decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational
modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview,
a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research.
RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and
coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary
perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities.
Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable
deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the
framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments
on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper
quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and
human evaluations with fewer comments.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are advancing automated research toward
end-to-end scientific workflows spanning literature review, experimental
analysis, and paper writing ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Yamada et
al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). Recent
work further incorporates peer review into this loop ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Weng et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)), making automated
review central to research quality control. While LLM reviewers can
provide useful critiques and well-supported feedback ([Liang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib14); [Idahl and Ahmadi, 2025](#bib.bib16); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)), reliable final judgments still require
cross-validating from multiple perspectives, resolving conflicts, and
filtering unsupported comments.

Figure 1: When reviewing papers, (a) relies on a single agent with
manual verification, (b) aggregates independent reviews with limited
interaction, whereas (c) supports specialized multi-agent debate,
comment revision and voting to produce a robust and traceable report.

Existing automated review methods lack modeling of peer review
mechanisms in the real world. Single-model judgments may miss key
claims ([Ou et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Shin et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)),
while multi-agent approaches with role specialization and tools ([D’Arcy
et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Goyal et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)) often rely
on simple aggregation, lacking clear responsibility boundaries and
overlooking role and expertise differences of experts, thus producing
low-quality and redundant feedback, as shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").
Therefore, we formulate automated paper review as a computational
modeling of peer-review mechanisms, where independent judgments are
cross-examined to produce collective decisions with adoption rationales.

Building on this perspective, we propose a deliberative multi-agent
framework RoundtableReview, which models automated paper review as a
process from evidence-grounding to collective decision-making.
RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and
assigns six academic and industry reviewers with complementary
perspectives. Each reviewer conducts independent review according to the
primary perspective, secondary perspective and explicit responsibility
boundaries, with dedicated retrieval sources supporting the primary
perspective. Reviewers then cross-examine and revise comments through
roundtable discussion. Surviving comments are selected through voting
weighted by role authority and scenario relevance, and a review chairman
synthesizes them into the final review.

We then evaluate RoundtableReview on PaperWritingBench ([Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)) with two writing backbones, PaperOrchestra ([Song et
al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) and ARIS ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)),
against GLM-5.2 ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)) and AI
Scientist-v2 ([Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) using longitudinal and
horizontal comparisons, automatic evaluators, and blind human
evaluation. Despite generating fewer comments than the baselines,
RoundtableReview consistently improves both literature review quality
and overall paper quality, with notable gains in scientific depth,
technical execution, and presentation of evidence. Ablation studies
demonstrate that both multi-role discussion and weighted voting
contribute to the effectiveness of the framework. The main contributions
are as follows:

- •
  Reconceptualizing automated paper review as a collaborative
  deliberative process, facilitating traceable cross-examination and
  collective decision-making
- •
  Proposing RoundtableReview that incorporates semantic slots,
  specialized reviewer roles, retrieval-based perspectives,
  deliberation, weighted voting, and chair synthesis
- •
  Evaluating RoundtableReview with two writing backbones and review
  baselines through automatic and human evaluation, demonstrating
  improvements in paper quality

## 2 Related Work

We review prior studies in three research areas closely related to our
work: automated research, scientific review, and multi-agent debate.

#### Automated Research

Automated research has evolved from task-specific agents to closed-loop
workflows covering ideation, experimentation, writing, and review ([Lu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Baek et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).
PaperOrchestra ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), ARIS ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)), and AutoResearchClaw ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23))
further advance self-improvement and long-horizon research workflow. Yet
weakly validated reviews may misguide revision and limit research
quality ([Tang and Yang, 2026](#bib.bib24); [Fei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25)). We address the above bottleneck through deliberation
and review-guided revision.

#### Scientific Review

Scientific review has progressed toward more criteria-based and
human-aligned evaluation. LLM reviewers can identify certain issues
raised by human ([Liang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib14)), while OpenReviewer
and DeepReview improve specificity through specialized training and
reasoning ([Idahl and Ahmadi, 2025](#bib.bib16); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)). However, alignment gains from guidelines and
retrieval vary across models ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Chen et
al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), while limited modeling of real-world peer
review mechanisms may lead to unsupported or low-quality critiques ([Ou
et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Shin et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Dycke and
Gurevych, 2026](#bib.bib20)).

#### Multi-Agent Debate

Multi-agent debate improves reasoning through argument exchange,
negotiation, and heterogeneous interaction ([Du et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Liang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib22)), enabling agents to critically examine competing
perspectives, resolve disagreements, and refine their judgments through
iterative discussion. However, its effectiveness depends heavily on
interaction design and the coordination of diverse agent
perspectives ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)).  [Kaesberg et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib30) highlight how voting and consensus protocols shape
collective reasoning outcomes. In scientific review, MARG and
ScholarPeer introduce role specialization and structured
interaction ([D’Arcy et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Goyal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)), whereas RoundtableReview explicitly models
real-world peer-review mechanisms through evidence-grounded
deliberation, systematically tracking how comments are challenged,
revised, and incorporated into collective decisions.

Figure 2: The overall framework consists of three parts: (1) paper
decomposition into eight semantic slots; (2) six role-specialized
reviewer agents and one chair agent; (3) a collaborative multi-agent
review process for transforming independent comments into collective
reviews through debate, revision, voting, and comment synthesis.

## 3 Method

We propose RoundtableReview, a multi-agent peer review framework
designed to enhance automated research. Each paper is decomposed into
eight semantic slots for independent review by six role-specialized
reviewers with distinct expertise. Their initial reviews are refined
through roundtable deliberation, followed by dynamic weighted voting.
Review chairman summarizes the accepted comments into a consolidated
report. The overall framework is shown in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Multi-Agent Debate ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

### 3.1 Task Formulation

We formalize automated paper review as a deliberative decision-making
process. Given a paper $`x`$, RoundtableReview produces a final review
report $`y`$ and an audit trail $`\mathcal{T}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
x\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}^{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}^{*}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\rightarrow(y,\mathcal{T}),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{Z}`$ denotes semantic slots; $`\mathcal{O}^{0}`$ and
$`\mathcal{O}^{*}`$ denote opinions before and after deliberation,
respectively; $`\mathcal{D}`$ denotes discussion records;
$`\mathcal{V}`$ denotes the weighted voting results used to select
comments; and $`\mathcal{T}`$ records evidence, discussion, comment
evolution, and voting decisions.

### 3.2 Semantic Slots

To reduce claim-evidence misalignment, we structure content by semantic
function instead of section headings. Each paper is mapped into eight
slots: background and motivation (Why), problem and objective (What),
related work and research landscape (Situation), method and technical
approach (How), experiments and evidence (Proof), value and impact
(Value), risks and limitations (Risk), and resources and reproducibility
(Resource). For each slot $`z_{k}`$, the parser records relevant text
spans and locations while retaining full paper access. The process
supports role-specific evidence retrieval while mitigating opinion
convergence induced by repeated full paper reading.

### 3.3 Role-Specialized Reviewers

To obtain complementary assessments while controlling for backbone
capability, we instantiate six specialized reviewer roles on the same
model. Each role adopts one primary perspective supported by retrieval
aligned with its responsibilities and two secondary perspectives without
external retrieval. Each role also prioritizes semantic slots relevant
to its assessment focus. This design combines assessments grounded in
external evidence with broader coverage of paper quality.
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Role-Specialized Reviewers ‣ 3 Method ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
summarizes the perspectives, priority slots, and retrieval sources
assigned to each role.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Role | Primary Perspective | Secondary Perspectives | Priority Slots | Retrieval Source |
| Academic Expert | research foresight | contribution & differentiation | Why, What, Situation, How, Value | arXiv surveys |
| Academic Star | innovation and depth | methodological rigor & soundness | What, How, Proof | arXiv frontier papers |
| Cross-domain Researcher | cross-domain transfer validity | completeness & generalizability | What, How, Value | out-of-domain arXiv papers |
| Strategic Leader | strategic value & goal alignment | risk controllability & research capacity | Why, What, How, Value, Risk | CAPC-CG policy corpus |
| Industry Manager | compliance with standards | logical soundness & clarity | What, How, Proof | EPO OPS |
| Technical Expert | soundness & feasibility | complexity & resource allocation | How, Proof, Resource | GitHub REST API |
| Review Chairman | Synthesizes approved comments without reviewing or voting. |  | All slots | — |

Table 1: Reviewer roles, perspectives, priority slots, and retrieval
sources in RoundtableReview.

The academic roles include an academic expert, an academic star, and a
cross-domain researcher, focusing on research foresight, depth of
innovation, and cross-domain transferability. These roles retrieve
public papers through the arXiv API¹¹ 1
[https://arxiv.org/](https://arxiv.org/): survey papers for the academic
expert, frontier research excluding surveys for the academic star, and
out-of-domain papers for the cross-domain researcher. The industry roles
comprise a strategic leader, an industry manager, and a technical
expert, focusing on strategic value, standards compliance, and
engineering feasibility, respectively. They retrieve sources from
CAPC-CG policy corpus ([Sun et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)), the European
Patent Office (EPO) OPS API²² 2
[https://www.epo.org/en](https://www.epo.org/en), and the GitHub REST
API³³ 3 [https://github.com/](https://github.com/).

### 3.4 Independent Review

To reduce conformity and premature consensus, all agents first review
independently. Each agent follows its role identity, primary and
secondary perspectives, priority semantic slots, and predefined
instructions, with retrieved evidence added only for the primary
perspective, and each agent produces at most three comments. We further
introduce a “honesty protection” rule: limitations explicitly
acknowledged by the authors in Limitations or Future Work cannot be
restated as weaknesses. We represent each initial comment as:

|     |                                |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       o_{i}^{0}=(u_{i},c_{i},a_{i}),
       ```                             |     | (2) |

where $`u_{i}`$, $`c_{i}`$, and $`a_{i}`$ respectively indicate the
issue, rationale, and suggested revision.

### 3.5 Roundtable Discussion

To improve the quality of initial comments and address role-specific
blind spots, we structure roundtable discussion into two stages:
scrutiny across roles and comment refinement based on feedback. During
cross-role scrutiny, each agent evaluates all comments from the other
roles and labels them as agreement, needs-improvement, or disagreement;
the latter two require explicit justifications. Comments opposed by at
least three of their five peer reviewers are discarded.

During comment refinement, the remaining comments are returned to their
proposers, who retain, revise, or withdraw them based on the discussion
feedback. Only retained and revised comments proceed to weighted voting
session. Further details are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A More Details of Roundtable Discussion ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

### 3.6 Dynamic Weighted Voting

Each agent automatically assigns $`+1`$ to its prior agreement comments.
For other comments, it votes based on the revised content, with at most
three positive votes in total. All comments not receiving a positive
vote from that agent receive $`-1`$.

To account for differences in role expertise and scenario relevance, we
apply dynamic weighted voting to comments. The vote is weighted by role
authority $`\alpha_{j}`$ and scenario relevance $`\beta_{j,d}`$, where
$`\alpha_{j}`$ captures the relative influence assigned to agent $`j`$
based on its role expertise, and $`\beta_{j,d}`$ reflects the alignment
between its role and the evaluation priorities of scenario $`d`$. The
weighted vote score is computed as follows:

|     |                                                            |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       S(o_{i}^{*})=\sum_{j\neq p(i)}\alpha_{j}\beta_{j,d}v_{ji},
       ```                                                         |     | (3) |

where $`v_{ji}\in\{-1,+1\}`$ and $`p(i)`$ denotes the proposer, comments
with $`S(o_{i}^{*})\leq 0`$ are discarded.

### 3.7 Chair Synthesis

An independent chair synthesizes comments approved through voting into
the final report without participating in previous sessions. Using
weighted scores, discussion records, and evidence anchors, it merges
duplicates and prioritizes the remaining comments. The report contains
an overall assessment and 3-6 recommendations. Complete prompt
specifications for all agents and all stages of the framework are
provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B RoundtableReview: Detailed Prompt ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Settings

#### Dataset

PaperWritingBench ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) is adopted, with 20
papers randomly sampled from each of CVPR 2025 and ICLR 2025, totaling
40 papers. Each sample provides a research idea, experiment logs,
conference template, submission guidelines, and visual assets for paper
generation.

#### Implementation Details

RoundtableReview uses GLM-5.2 via API with temperature = 1.0 and top_p =
0.95. We set max_tokens to 120,000 and limit the context window to
1,500,000 characters. The authority weights $`\alpha_{j}`$ for the
technical expert, strategic leader, industry manager, cross-domain
researcher, academic expert, and academic star roles are set to 1.1,
1.5, 1.0, 1.1, 1.5, and 1.0, respectively. The relevance weights
$`\beta_{j,\text{paper}}`$ are set to 1.2 for academic roles and 0.9 for
industry roles. These weights were selected through parameter tuning.
The total cost across all experiments and evaluations is approximately
\$2000 USD.

For the retrieval sources supporting the primary perspective of each
agent, the academic expert retrieves 5 arXiv surveys, while the academic
star retrieves 8 arXiv papers and retains up to 5 non-survey research
papers. The cross-domain researcher retrieves 5 arXiv papers. For these
agents, HTML full texts are truncated to 40,000 characters, with
abstracts used only when full text retrieval fails. The strategic leader
retrieves 10 skeleton entries from the CAPC-CG policy corpus. The
industry manager retrieves 5 European and international patents via the
EPO OPS API, each truncated to the 3,000 characters. The technical
expert retrieves 10 GitHub repositories ranked by stars, using their
descriptions and metadata.

#### Backbones, Review Baselines, and Ablations

We use PaperOrchestra ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), reproduced from
its public code with Gemini 3.1 Pro, and ARIS ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)), using its paper-writing skill with Claude Sonnet 4.6.
For both backbone agents, we retain the original parameter settings.
They generate R1 from identical inputs, then revise it into R2 based on
review feedback, and all review methods share the same R1 input.

We compare against two review baselines: GLM-5.2 ([Zeng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4)) and the review component of AI Scientist-v2
(AIS-v2) ([Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). In addition, we evaluate
two ablated variants of RoundtableReview: parallel review omits
deliberation and retains only independent reviews ($`w/o`$
deliberation), while equal voting sets $`\alpha_{j}=\beta_{j,d}=1`$,
removing both role and relevance weighting ($`w/o`$ weighting).

### 4.2 Evaluation Method and Metrics

We evaluate literature review quality and overall paper quality through
automatic and human evaluation, and automatic evaluation uses both LLMs
and reviewer agents, following [Song et al. (2026)](#bib.bib3).

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Backbone | Judge | Comparison | Literature Review Quality |  |  |  | Paper Quality |  |  |  |  |  |

#### Evaluation Metrics

Our evaluation places greater emphasis on overall paper quality, with
literature review quality serving as a complementary measure. Overall
paper quality covers five dimensions: scientific depth, technical
execution, logical flow, clarity of writing, and presentation of
evidence. Literature review quality covers three dimensions:
organization and writing, positioning and novelty, and relevance and
focus. More details are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C More details of Evaluation Metrics ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

#### Bidirectional Side-by-Side Comparison

To mitigate LLM positional bias, each pair of papers is evaluated in
both AB/BA orders, with the labeled as a win (two wins, or one win and
one tie), a tie (one win and one loss, or two ties), or a loss. Votes
are aggregated across the three literature review quality and five paper
quality dimensions, and the overall result is their average. Evaluation
uses three LLMs (claude-fable-5, gpt-5.6-sol, and qwen3.8-max) and two
reviewer agents (ScholarPeer ([Goyal et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)) and
AutoResearchClaw ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23))) under identical
settings. We use two complementary evaluation settings: longitudinal
evaluation compares R1 and R2 from the same review pipeline to measure
revision gains, while horizontal evaluation compares R2 manuscripts
produced using different review methods to assess their relative
effectiveness.

#### Human Evaluation

We randomly sample six papers from ICLR and CVPR. One PhD researcher and
two graduate students voluntarily conduct anonymous side-by-side
comparisons of the revised R2 papers produced by our method and
baselines, following predefined guidelines and using the same metrics as
automatic evaluation.

### 4.3 Results

We investigate four key research questions.

1.  Q1:
    Does RoundtableReview consistently improve paper quality across
    different writing backbones and evaluators?
2.  Q2:
    Does RoundtableReview outperform review baselines in improving paper
    quality?
3.  Q3:
    How does review comment quantity affect revision effectiveness?
4.  Q4:
    How do multi-role discussion and weighted voting contribute to
    overall performance?

#### Longitudinal Evaluation Results (Q1)

As shown in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.6 Dynamic Weighted Voting ‣ 3 Method ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review"),
RoundtableReview improves paper quality from R1 to R2 across two writing
backbones and three LLM judges. For overall paper quality,
RoundtableReview achieves the highest R2 win rate in all settings,
outperforming both GLM-5.2 and AI Scientist-v2, with win rates of
92.5%-97.5% for ARIS and 87.5%-90.0% for PaperOrchestra. The gains are
particularly pronounced in scientific depth, technical execution, and
presentation of evidence. For overall literature review quality,
RoundtableReview achieves the highest performance across all three
judges under PaperOrchestra, while showing weaker results under ARIS,
likely reflecting differences in how the writing backbones utilize
review comments.

Figure 3: Longitudinal evaluation results comparing Round 1 (R1) and
Round 2 (R2) on literature review and paper quality: (a) Literature
review quality evaluated by ScholarPeer; (b) literature review quality
evaluated by AutoResearchClaw; (c) paper quality evaluated by
ScholarPeer; (d) paper quality evaluated by AutoResearchClaw.

Agent-based evaluation with ScholarPeer and AutoResearchClaw further
supports the effectiveness of RoundtableReview, as shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Longitudinal Evaluation Results (Q1) ‣ 4.3 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").
For overall paper quality, RoundtableReview achieves R2 win rates of
75.0%-92.5% across the two writing backbones, outperforming AI
Scientist-v2 in all settings and showing more consistent gains than
GLM-5.2. For overall literature review quality, RoundtableReview also
generally outperforms AI Scientist-v2 and exceeds GLM-5.2 in most
settings. Detailed scores for each subdimension of the agent-based
longitudinal evaluation are reported in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D More Longitudinal Evaluation Results ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

#### Horizontal Evaluation Results (Q2)

As demonstrated by the comparasion results presented in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Evaluation Method and Metrics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review"),
the advantages of RoundtableReview are primarily reflected in overall
paper quality. RoundtableReview outperforms AI Scientist-v2 across all
six backbone-judge combinations, with notable gains in scientific depth,
technical execution, and presentation of evidence. Compared with
GLM-5.2, RoundtableReview performs better with PaperOrchestra but worse
with ARIS. Nevertheless, GLM-5.2 yields smaller R1 to R2 gains in the
longitudinal evaluation, indicating that it is less effective than
RoundtableReview in improving the original paper.

Agent-based horizontal evaluation with ScholarPeer and AutoResearchClaw
further confirms the advantage of RoundtableReview in overall paper
quality, as shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Horizontal Evaluation Results (Q2) ‣ 4.3 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").
RoundtableReview outperforms AI Scientist-v2 across all settings, while
it performs better under ARIS and remains more closely matched with
GLM-5.2 under PaperOrchestra. For overall literature review quality,
RoundtableReview shows stronger performance under ARIS and variation
under PaperOrchestra, possibly reflecting greater evaluator sensitivity
in literature review assessment. Detailed scores for subdimensions of
the agent-based horizontal evaluation are reported in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E More Horizontal Evaluation Results ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

#### Human Evaluation Results

Human evaluation further validates the effectiveness of
RoundtableReview, as shown in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Horizontal Evaluation Results (Q2) ‣ 4.3 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").
Across two writing backbones and two baselines, RoundtableReview
consistently outperforms the baselines in both overall assessments and
all evaluation dimensions, demonstrating robust improvements across
different experimental settings. These gains span scientific depth,
technical execution, logical flow, writing clarity, and evidence
presentation, indicating broad improvements in manuscript quality.
Inter-annotator agreement yields a Fleiss’ kappa ([Fleiss,
1971](#bib.bib29)) of 0.087. Fleiss’ kappa and Cohen’s kappa ([Cohen,
1960](#bib.bib5)) statistics for human-LLM and human-agent agreement are
reported in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

#### Further Analysis of RoundtableReview (Q3)

As shown in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Further Analysis of RoundtableReview (Q3) ‣ 4.3 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review"),
RoundtableReview achieves stronger and more stable revision performance
with only 4.2-4.3 suggestions per paper on average, compared with
12.7-17.6 for the baselines. This highlights the comment efficiency of
RoundtableReview: multi-role discussion and collective selection
concentrate revision guidance into a smaller set of more effective
suggestions rather than relying on comment volume. In a few settings,
the stronger performance of the baselines may partly stem from retaining
a larger number of revision suggestions.

#### Ablation Study (Q4)

The longitudinal evaluation results in
Table [9](#A7.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix G Results of Ablation Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
of
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Results of Ablation Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
show that removing either the weighting mechanism or multi-role
discussion generally degrades overall performance. Removing the
weighting mechanism causes a modest drop, while removing multi-role
discussion exhibits stronger backbone dependence, with larger declines
under PaperOrchestra, particularly in overall paper quality and
technical dimensions. The horizontal evaluation results in
Table [10](#A7.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix G Results of Ablation Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
of
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Results of Ablation Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
further demonstrate consistent benefits from the weighting mechanism,
while the effect of multi-role discussion varies by backbone. Case
studies comparing excerpts from our method, AI-scientist-v2, and GLM-5.2
reviews are presented in
Table [11](#A8.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix H Case Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
of
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Case Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review").

## 5 Conclusion

We propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework that
models real-world peer review mechanisms for evidence-based and
traceable automated review. Our framework structures papers into
semantic slots and coordinates specialized reviewers through independent
review, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted
voting, and chair synthesis. Across two writing backbones, both
automatic and human evaluations demonstrate consistent improvements in
paper quality. Notably, RoundtableReview enhances review effectiveness
with fewer comments, highlighting its value in delivering more focused
and impactful feedback.

## Limitations

Our framework remains an approximation of real-world peer review to a
certain extent. Prompt-based role specialization, single-round
deliberation, and predefined voting weights simplify the diversity of
reviewer expertise and the dynamics of multi-round discussion.
Additionally, although our evaluation combines automatic and human
evaluation across multiple settings, the number of human annotators
remains limited. Future work may explore richer reviewer and
larger-scale expert evaluation in broader research domains. Although
evaluated in paper review, RoundtableReview may also be adapted to
project reviews, proposal evaluations, and related applications.

## Ethical Considerations

This study relies on existing LLMs for paper review, discussion, and
evaluation, therefore inherits common risks of LLM-based systems,
including inaccurate, unsupported, or inappropriate comment.
RoundtableReview also relies on external retrieval sources, including
public papers, patents, and policy documents. Although these sources do
not contain offensive content, the retrieved information may contain
errors or biases. All models, datasets, and external resources should be
used in accordance with their applicable licenses, terms of use, and
data policies.

Role specialization, retrieval, and weighted voting may introduce bias
related to discipline, language, expertise, or research conventions. To
improve transparency, RoundtableReview preserves evidence sources,
discussion records, comment revisions, and voting results, allowing
users to inspect how recommendations are formed. Broader evaluation
across research domains, languages, and reviewer populations remains
necessary before deployment in real world.

RoundtableReview is intended to support manuscript improvement rather
than replace human judgment in paper acceptance, academic assessment, or
other high-impact decisions. Automated reviews should therefore be
interpreted as decision-support signals rather than authoritative
judgments, with meaningful human oversight retained in consequential
settings. Finally, although this study does not train new foundation
models, multi-agent reviewing, retrieval, and repeated evaluation incur
additional computational and environmental costs.

## Appendix A More Details of Roundtable Discussion

Each role may agree with at most five comments and must disagree with at
least three, with the rest labeled needs-improvement. Excess agreement
judgments are converted to needs-improvement, and insufficient
disagreement judgments are supplemented from needs-improvement.

## Appendix B RoundtableReview: Detailed Prompt

The review pipeline consists of six parallel reviewer agents and one
chairman agent, operating across four stages: (1) independent review,
(2) structured peer discussion, (3) final report aggregation by the
chairman. Stages 2 and 3 use identical prompt templates across all six
reviewer agents; only the agent name and role_description field are
substituted per role.
Section [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Agent Overview ‣ Appendix B RoundtableReview: Detailed Prompt ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
provides an agent overview;
Sections [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Stage 1: Independent Review ‣ Appendix B RoundtableReview: Detailed Prompt ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")-[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Stage 3: Report Aggregation (Chairman) ‣ Appendix B RoundtableReview: Detailed Prompt ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
give the complete prompts for each stage.

## Appendix C More details of Evaluation Metrics

Literature review quality covers three dimensions: organization and
writing, for the structure and presentation of the Introduction and
Related Work; positioning and novelty, for how well the research gap and
novelty are motivated by prior work; and relevance and focus, for the
relevance and focus of citations and discussion.

Overall paper quality covers five dimensions: scientific depth, for
reasoning rigor and experimental completeness; technical execution, for
implementation and experimental coverage; logical flow, for coherence
across sections; clarity of writing, for clarity and precision; and
presentation of evidence, for how well figures, tables, and results
support the claims. Both are assessed through longitudinal R1-R2 and
horizontal R2-R2 comparisons.

## Appendix D More Longitudinal Evaluation Results

We compare Round 1 (R1) and Round 2 (R2) across literature review and
paper quality dimensions using ScholarPeer and AutoResearchClaw. As
shown in
Figure [5](#A6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review"),
our method achieves consistent gains in positioning and novelty: R2 wins
account for 32.5–47.5% of comparisons across ARIS and PaperOrchestra,
whereas R1 wins account for only 5–10%. Organization and writing, and
relevance and focus, exhibit higher tie rates of 42.5–62.5% and mixed
directional preferences. These results suggest that revision improves
the positioning of the research more consistently than the organization
and focus of the literature review.

Improvements are broader for paper quality.
Figure [6](#A6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
shows that our method achieves R2 win rates of 90–97.5% in scientific
depth, exceeding both the GLM-5.2 and AIS-v2 conditions in every matched
setting. Technical execution also improves consistently, with R2 win
rates of 67.5–92.5%.
Figure [7](#A6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
further shows improvements in presentation of evidence, with R2 win
rates of 70–92.5%. Improvements in logical flow and writing clarity are
more dependent on the evaluator. ScholarPeer favors R2 in 77.5–87.5% of
these comparisons, while AutoResearchClaw reports R2 win rates of
47.5–62.5%, including several cases where R1 remains preferred. The
longitudinal results therefore indicate more consistent progress in
scientific substance and evidence presentation than in writing and
coherence.

## Appendix E More Horizontal Evaluation Results

We compare our method with the GLM-5.2 and AIS-v2 conditions at Round 2
(R2) within ARIS and PaperOrchestra.
Figure [8](#A6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
shows that the advantage in literature review quality varies across
dimensions and systems. Within ARIS, our method achieves win rates of
67.5–80% in organization and writing and 60–85% in relevance and focus,
but only 25–45% in positioning and novelty. Within PaperOrchestra,
positioning and novelty instead emerges as a relative strength, with win
rates of 50–62.5%. Organization and focus receive mixed judgments, with
AutoResearchClaw favoring the baselines in both dimensions.

For paper quality, the strongest advantages appear in comparisons
against AIS-v2. Across both systems and evaluators,
Figure [9](#A6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
shows win rates of 70–90% in scientific depth and 67.5–90% in technical
execution, while
Figure [10](#A6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix F Human Assessment Consistency ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")
reports win rates of 72.5–87.5% in presentation of evidence. Comparisons
against GLM-5.2 are more mixed, particularly within PaperOrchestra,
where the baseline remains competitive in scientific depth and technical
execution. Writing clarity and logical flow also reveal substantial
variation across systems: our method wins 65–90% of comparisons within
ARIS, whereas its win rates within PaperOrchestra fall to 10–45% under
AutoResearchClaw. These differences indicate that the benefits of our
method depend on both the research system and the evaluation criterion.

## Appendix G Results of Ablation Study

We assess deliberation and weighting through R1–R2 comparisons
(Table [9](#A7.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix G Results of Ablation Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review"))
and direct R2–R2 comparisons
(Table [10](#A7.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix G Results of Ablation Study ‣ Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review")).
The full model is more often preferred on overall paper quality than the
variant without deliberation across both backbones, and outperforms both
ablations within PaperOrchestra. The benefits of weighting and effects
on literature review quality vary across settings.

## Appendix H Case Study

This case study highlights the advantage of RoundtableReview in
translating targeted feedback into concrete, reproducible revisions. AI
Scientist-v2 requests general technical clarification, but its revision
introduces a similarity threshold and top-$`k`$ sampling, altering the
original nearest-neighbor procedure. GLM-5.2 suggests broader
noise-modeling extensions, yet the corresponding passage remains
unchanged. In contrast, RoundtableReview identifies specific
reproducibility gaps and elicits a revision specifying the BERT encoder
and representation, cosine similarity, an explicit label-selection
equation, corruption probability, and binary-answer handling, with a
reference to complete pseudocode. The revision also clarifies that no
similarity threshold is used, preserving the original nearest-neighbor
formulation. These improvements illustrate how RoundtableReview produces
more actionable feedback and clearer methodological specifications while
maintaining fidelity to the stated method.

Original Semantic Noise Simulation Standard noise simulation uses random
label shuffling, which produces medically implausible mislabeling (e.g.,
“X-ray” for a pathology question). We propose a more realistic
simulation: for each answer $`a_{k}`$, we encode all possible answers
using a pre-trained BERT model and replace $`a_{k}`$ with its nearest
neighbor in BERT embedding space, creating a semantically plausible but
incorrect label. Figure 3 illustrates that semantic noise pairs retain
feature-space proximity, unlike random noise. Noise protocols We
evaluate under three noise conditions: 10% Semantic Noise, 20% Semantic
Noise (via our BERT-proximity simulation), and 20% Random Noise (uniform
label shuffling). Test sets remain clean in all settings. The Upper
Bound is performance with clean training labels (VQA-RAD: 79.13%;
PathVQA: 72.61% overall). AI-scientist-v2 Review Comment The paper lacks
clarity in explaining certain technical details, such as the
architecture and hyperparameter choices for the Noisy Label Refinement
(NLR) module and the setup of the semantic noise simulation protocol.
Revised Paragraph Semantic Noise Simulation Unchanged from the original.
Noise protocols We evaluate under three noise conditions: 10% Semantic
Noise, 20% Semantic Noise (via our BERT-proximity simulation), and 20%
Random Noise (uniform label shuffling). The semantic noise simulation
protocol constructs corrupted labels by replacing the ground-truth
answer with its nearest neighbor in BERT embedding space, subject to the
constraint that the replacement is semantically plausible (cosine
similarity $`>0.6`$) but distinct from the correct answer. Concretely,
for each training sample selected for corruption, we encode all
candidate answers with a frozen BERT encoder, retrieve the top-$`k`$
($`k=5`$) nearest neighbors of the ground-truth answer embedding, and
sample the replacement uniformly from this set. This reflects realistic
annotation errors where a clinician’s incorrect label is at least
semantically adjacent to the correct one (e.g., “left” vs. “right”,
“high magnification” vs. “low magnification”). Test sets remain clean in
all settings. The Upper Bound is performance with clean training labels
(VQA-RAD: 79.13%; PathVQA: 72.61% overall). GLM-5.2 Review Comment The
semantic noise simulation protocol, while a valuable contribution, is
limited to nearest-neighbor replacement in BERT space. Real medical
annotation errors may involve hierarchical relationships (e.g., ‘lobar
pneumonia’ vs ‘bronchopneumonia’) or multi-attribute confusion. The
protocol could be enriched with multiple noise levels or structured
noise patterns. Revised Paragraph Semantic Noise Simulation. Unchanged
from the original. Noise protocols. Unchanged from the original. Ours
Review Comment The method description lacks critical algorithmic
details—including the diffusion noise schedule, exact Robust Focal Loss
formulation, EMA blending formula, and the semantic noise simulation
protocol’s BERT variant, similarity metric, and threshold
parameters—preventing independent reproduction; the authors should
provide complete mathematical definitions, step-by-step pseudocode, and
hyperparameter sensitivity ranges in supplementary material to ensure
graduate-level reproducibility. Revised Paragraph Semantic Noise
Simulation. Standard noise simulation uses random label shuffling, which
produces medically implausible mislabeling (e.g., “X-ray” for a
pathology question). We propose a more realistic simulation: for each
answer $`a_{k}`$, we encode all possible answers using BERT-Base
(\[CLS\] token of the final layer, $`\mathbb{R}^{768}`$) and replace
$`a_{k}`$ with its nearest neighbor in cosine similarity space.
Formally, the noisy label is
$`a_{k}^{*}=\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}\limits_{a\neq a_{k},\,a\in\mathcal{A}}\cos(e_{a_{k}},e_{a})`$,
where the nearest neighbor is taken as a hard selection (no similarity
threshold; see Sec. A.1 for complete pseudocode). With probability
$`\eta`$ (noise ratio), we replace $`a_{k}`$ with $`a_{k}^{*}`$;
otherwise $`a_{k}`$ is kept. For closed-end Yes/No questions, symmetric
binary noise is used since the two-class vocabulary does not admit
meaningful semantic nearest-neighbor computation. Figure 3 illustrates
that semantic noise pairs retain feature-space proximity, unlike random
noise. Noise protocols. Unchanged from the original.
````
